title: Parliament takes up bill to speed rooftop and institutional solar
excerpt: The Special Solar Power Installation Bill allows limited tendering up to Tk 5 crore without e-GP. A committee has three working days to report.
content:
Power and Energy Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood introduced the Special Solar Power Installation Bill, 2026 in Parliament on Tuesday, 10 November, The Daily Star reported. The bill replaces an ordinance issued on 19 October. It was sent to the parliamentary committee, which must report within three working days.

What the bill does

  • Allows solar systems to be installed on a priority basis under an operating-cost (OPEX) model, where a provider installs and the user pays for power.
  • Lets institutions with their own funds or steady revenue buy systems outright (CAPEX model), subject to financial viability.
  • Requires three-way agreements between consumers, service providers and the authorities.
  • Allows limited tendering for CAPEX goods and services up to Tk 5 crore, without the e-GP online procurement system.
  • Sets up a National Policy Council and district technical and coordination committees.
  • Makes theft of power or equipment from these systems punishable by up to three years in prison, a fine of up to Tk 50,000, or both.

The debate

Jamaat-e-Islami MP Nazibur Rahman said the ordinance bypassed Parliament. Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman replied that the President may issue ordinances when Parliament is not sitting and that, under Article 93(1), Parliament cannot question the President’s satisfaction in doing so, the newspaper reported.

Why it matters

The bill follows the National Renewable Energy Development Strategy 2026-2030, adopted in July, and fits with calls at COP31 for more renewable investment. A Change Initiative study this month found most energy-sector climate finance has come as loans and recommended rooftop solar on factories and institutions. Schools, hospitals and NGO offices could use the OPEX model to install solar without upfront cost. Governance groups may question the exemption from e-GP, which was introduced to make public procurement more transparent.

What to watch

  • The committee report, due within three working days, and any changes to the procurement exemption.
  • Rules setting out who can act as a service provider and how tariffs are set.
